clinicalPearls: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory state, considered a form of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, characterised by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells.
It most commonly complicates rheumatic conditions, especially systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, but can be triggered by infection or malignancy.
Suspect it when a child with an underlying inflammatory disease develops persistent high fever, worsening general condition, and hepatosplenomegaly.
A characteristic and counterintuitive clue is falling blood counts (cytopenias) and a paradoxically falling or normalising ESR despite active inflammation.
Markedly elevated ferritin is a hallmark laboratory feature and useful for both suspicion and monitoring.
Other typical findings include high triglycerides, low fibrinogen, deranged liver function, and coagulopathy, sometimes with overt bleeding.
Bone marrow examination may show haemophagocytosis, but a normal marrow does not exclude the diagnosis and treatment should not be delayed for it.
This is a medical emergency requiring rapid immunosuppression to interrupt the cytokine storm before multi-organ failure develops.
reference.pathophysiology: MAS results from defective downregulation of the immune response, with impaired cytotoxic function of natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. This allows persistent activation and proliferation of T cells and well-differentiated macrophages (histiocytes), which phagocytose blood cells and release a flood of pro-inflammatory cytokines. This cytokine storm produces sustained fever, cytopenias from marrow phagocytosis and suppression, hepatic dysfunction, coagulopathy resembling disseminated intravascular coagulation, and progressive multi-organ damage.
additionalDifferentials: Flare of the underlying rheumatic disease
Systemic infection (EBV and other viruses, intracellular pathogens)
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin (very high levels are characteristic and trended for response)
Full blood count to detect evolving cytopenias
Fibrinogen, D-dimer, and full coagulation profile
Liver function tests and lactate dehydrogenase
Soluble interleukin-2 receptor (soluble CD25) and natural killer cell function where available
Bone marrow aspirate to look for haemophagocytosis when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Rapidly progressive multi-organ dysfunction from cytokine storm (EMERGENCY)
Persistent high fever with deteriorating clinical state
Falling cell counts across multiple lineages
Falling fibrinogen with rising ferritin and clinical bleeding
Progression toward disseminated intravascular coagulation or shock
reference.prognosis: MAS carries significant mortality if unrecognised, but early aggressive immunosuppression can be life-saving and many children recover; outcome depends on prompt diagnosis, control of the trigger, and reversal of organ dysfunction before it becomes irreversible.
pitfalls: Being falsely reassured by a falling or normal ESR, which can accompany the low fibrinogen of MAS
Interpreting the picture solely as a disease flare or sepsis and delaying specific treatment
Waiting for bone marrow confirmation of haemophagocytosis before starting therapy
Underappreciating how quickly the condition can progress to coagulopathy and organ failure
Not monitoring ferritin and blood counts closely to track response
management: Prompt immunosuppression is life-saving, with high-dose pulsed corticosteroids (methylprednisolone) as first-line therapy, escalated early

Interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra and/or ciclosporin for inadequate response, reserving the anti-interferon-gamma agent emapalumab or an etoposide-based haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis protocol for refractory disease

Identify and treat the trigger by controlling the underlying rheumatic disease (especially systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis), treating precipitating infection with appropriate antimicrobials, or addressing malignancy
Intensive supportive care including management of the disseminated intravascular coagulation-like coagulopathy with blood products, organ support and correction of metabolic derangement
Serial monitoring of ferritin, blood counts, fibrinogen, triglycerides, liver function and coagulation to gauge treatment response
Multidisciplinary care with paediatric rheumatology, haematology and intensive care, escalating to critical care early for multi-organ dysfunction
